body.statement: For every \(k\ge0\) and \(n\ge2k+4\), \(d_{e^{\star}}(G^{\star}_{k,n})=2^{k+1}\) and therefore \[D_k(n)=2^{k+1}.\] One original coefficient \(e^{\star}\) separates all branches on a nonempty Zariski-open covariance set.
body.proof_tex:
Put \(d=k+1\) and \(N=2d+2=2k+4\).  We first use the \(N\)-vertex member of \(\mathrm{def:attaining\mbox{-}family}\).  Its directed edge set has the \(3d\) arrows
\[
 0\to P_i,\qquad 0\to Q_i,\qquad P_i\to h
 \quad (1\leq i\leq d).
\]
The supplied set \(T\) consists of the first \(2d\) arrows and \(P_1\to h\).  Consequently
\[
 |T|=2d+1=N-1,
 \qquad
 D\setminus T=\{P_i\to h:2\leq i\leq d\},
 \qquad
 |D\setminus T|=d-1=k.
\tag{1}
\]
Every nonroot vertex has exactly one incoming arrow in \(T\), every vertex is reached from \(0\), and the order consisting of \(0\), then the \(P_i,Q_i\), and then \(h\) is topological.  Thus \(T\) is a rooted spanning arborescence, the directed support is acyclic, and \(e^{\star}=P_1\to h\) is present.  By \(\mathrm{def:graph\mbox{-}class}\),
\[
 (G^{\star}_{k,N},T,e^{\star})\in\mathcal G_{N,k}.
\tag{2}
\]

We next exhibit a regular fiber with \(2^d\) points.  Choose rational numbers \(h_i>0\) and \(b_i\) satisfying \(b_i^2>4h_i\), and put \(H_0=\operatorname{diag}(h_1,\ldots,h_d)\).  Let \(H\) be a rational symmetric positive-definite matrix, sufficiently close to \(H_0\), with diagonal \((h_1,\ldots,h_d)\); below we impose one further generic condition on its off-diagonal entries.  In the vertex order \((0,P_1,\ldots,P_d,Q_1,\ldots,Q_d,h)\), set
\[
 \Sigma^{\star}=
 \begin{pmatrix}
  1&0&0&1\\
  0&H&H&0\\
  0&H&C_0I_d&b\\
  1&0&b^{\mathsf T}&M
 \end{pmatrix},
 \qquad b=(b_1,\ldots,b_d)^{\mathsf T}.
\tag{3}
\]
Choose the rational number \(C_0\) so that \(C_0I_d-H\succ0\).  The Schur complement of \(H\) in the principal \((P,Q)\)-block is \(C_0I_d-H\), so that block is positive definite.  The block indexed by \((0,P,Q)\) is therefore positive definite as well.  Choosing the rational number \(M\) larger than the final Schur-complement threshold gives
\[
 \Sigma^{\star}\succ0.
\tag{4}
\]

Write
\[
 a_i=\lambda_{0P_i},\qquad
 c_i=\lambda_{0Q_i},\qquad
 z_i=\lambda_{P_i h},\qquad
 z=(z_1,\ldots,z_d)^{\mathsf T},\qquad
 x=-Hz.
\]
The missing bidirected pairs in \(\mathrm{def:attaining\mbox{-}family}\) are \(P_i\leftrightarrow Q_i\), \(P_i\leftrightarrow h\), and \(Q_i\leftrightarrow h\), for \(1\leq i\leq d\).  Direct substitution of (3) into the residual formula \(F_{ij}\) gives, in the order \((P_i,h)\), \((Q_i,h)\), and \((P_i,Q_i)\),
\[
 0=-a_i-(Hz)_i,
 \qquad
 0=b_i-c_i-(Hz)_i,
 \qquad
 0=h_i+a_ic_i.
\tag{5}
\]
Since \(H\) is invertible, (5) is equivalent to
\[
 a_i=x_i,
 \qquad
 c_i=x_i+b_i,
 \qquad
 x_i^2+b_ix_i+h_i=0
 \quad(1\leq i\leq d),
 \qquad
 z=-H^{-1}x.
\tag{6}
\]
The discriminant of the \(i\)-th quadratic is \(b_i^2-4h_i>0\).  Hence (6) has exactly \(2^d\) solutions, all real.  Under the invertible linear change \(z\mapsto x=-Hz\), the residual Jacobian with respect to \((a,c,z)\) is nonsingular exactly when
\[
 \det(H)\prod_{i=1}^d(2x_i+b_i)\ne0.
\tag{7}
\]
Indeed, after the change of variables the three equations for index \(i\) have Jacobian determinant, up to sign, \(a_i+c_i=2x_i+b_i\).  At every solution,
\[
 (2x_i+b_i)^2=b_i^2-4h_i>0,
\]
and \(\det(H)>0\).  Thus all \(2^d\) points are reduced.  For each point define
\[
 \Omega=(I_N-\Lambda)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{\star}(I_N-\Lambda).
\tag{8}
\]
Equations (5) say exactly that the entries of (8) at the missing bidirected pairs vanish.  The topological order above makes \(I_N-\Lambda\) unit triangular and hence invertible.  Equation (4) and congruence in (8) then imply \(\Omega\succ0\).  Thus every one of the \(2^d\) residual solutions is a real positive-definite source lift with the required support.

We may choose \(H\) so that the original coefficient \(z_1=\lambda_{e^{\star}}\) has different values at all these points.  At \(H=H_0\), two solutions having different first quadratic roots already have different values \(z_1=-x_1/h_1\).  If two branch vectors \(x\ne x'\) have the same first coordinate, choose \(j>1\) with \(x_j\ne x'_j\) and set
\[
 H(s)=H_0+s(E_{1j}+E_{j1}).
\]
Differentiating \(-H(s)^{-1}x\) at \(s=0\) yields
\[
 \left.\frac{d}{ds}\bigl(z_1(x)-z_1(x')\bigr)\right|_{s=0}
 =\frac{x_j-x'_j}{h_1h_j}\ne0.
\tag{9}
\]
For each pair of branch vectors, equality of their first coordinates after applying \(-H^{-1}\) is therefore a proper algebraic condition on the off-diagonal entries of \(H\).  There are finitely many pairs.  Their union cannot contain a Euclidean neighborhood of \(H_0\); rational matrices are dense in that neighborhood.  We consequently choose the rational \(H\) in (3) outside this union while retaining positive definiteness.  Then all \(2^d\) values of \(z_1\) are distinct.

We now prove that the displayed points give the generic coordinate degree, rather than merely a special-fiber count.  There are \(3d\) directed coordinates and exactly \(3d\) missing-bidirected residual equations.  Since the family allows every other bidirected pair,
\[
 |D|+|B|+|V|
 =3d+\left(\binom N2-3d\right)+N
 =\frac{N(N+1)}2.
\tag{10}
\]
Let \(M_0=N(N+1)/2\), and replace the independent covariance coordinates in (3) by \(\Sigma^{\star}+\xi\), where the \(M_0\) entries of \(\xi\) are independent indeterminates.  At any one of the regular points above, seek the directed-coordinate vector \(v=(a,c,z)\) as a formal series
\[
 v(\xi)=v_0+\sum_{r\geq1}v_r(\xi),
\]
with \(v_r\) homogeneous of degree \(r\) in \(\xi\).  The homogeneous degree-\(r\) part of the residual equations is
\[
 J(v_0)v_r=-R_r(\xi,v_1,\ldots,v_{r-1}),
\tag{11}
\]
where \(J(v_0)\) is the residual Jacobian and the right-hand side is determined by lower degrees.  Condition (7) makes \(J(v_0)\) invertible, so (11) recursively gives one and only one \(v_r\) for every \(r\).  This constructs a formal section of the covariance projection through each of the \(2^d\) points.

By \(\mathrm{thm:incidence\mbox{-}localization}\), the incidence ring is the integral source ring and its covariance kernel is \(P_G\).  If \(f\in P_G\), substituting any formal section gives
\[
 f(\Sigma^{\star}+\xi)=0
 \quad\text{in }\mathbb C[[\xi]].
\]
Translation by the constant matrix \(\Sigma^{\star}\) is an injective automorphism of the covariance polynomial ring, and the entries of \(\xi\) are algebraically independent.  Hence \(f=0\), so
\[
 P_G=(0),\qquad
 K_G=\mathbb C(\sigma_{ij}:i\leq j).
\tag{12}
\]
The two fields in \(K_G\subseteq L\) have the same transcendence degree \(M_0\) by (10) and (12).  Since \(L\) is finitely generated over \(K_G\), it follows that \(L/K_G\) is finite.  Equivalently, the localized algebra \(A_K\) of \(\mathrm{thm:incidence\mbox{-}localization}\) is a zero-dimensional finitely generated integral \(K_G\)-algebra, hence is the finite field \(L\).

To bound its degree, partition the directed variables into the singleton blocks \(A_i=(a_i)\), the singleton blocks \(C_i=(c_i)\), and the block \(Z=(z_1,\ldots,z_d)\) of size \(d\).  The residual for \((P_i,Q_i)\) has block degrees bounded by \(A_i+C_i\), while those for \((P_i,h)\) and \((Q_i,h)\) have block degrees bounded by \(A_i+Z\) and \(C_i+Z\), respectively.  Thus the coefficient supplied by \(\mathrm{lem:multihomogeneous\mbox{-}bezout\mbox{-}isolated\mbox{-}bound}\) is
\[
 \left[\left(\prod_{i=1}^d A_iC_i\right)Z^d\right]
 \prod_{i=1}^d(A_i+C_i)(A_i+Z)(C_i+Z)=2^d.
\tag{13}
\]
For each \(i\), precisely two selections give \(A_iC_iZ\): one selects \(A_i,Z,C_i\), and the other selects \(C_i,A_i,Z\), from the three factors in their displayed order.  After extending scalars to an algebraic closure of \(K_G\), the scheme defined by the residuals is zero-dimensional and its length is \(\dim_{K_G}A_K=[L:K_G]\).  Applying the cited multihomogeneous bound to this square residual system, with multiplicities retained, gives
\[
 [L:K_G]\leq2^d.
\tag{14}
\]
This count uses the original residual polynomials, so it neither inverts a directed-coordinate expression nor removes a zero-over-zero point.

Conversely, each formal section constructed above defines a homomorphism from the incidence domain to \(\mathbb C[[\xi]]\) whose restriction to the covariance polynomial ring is the common injective translation map.  Its kernel has height zero: its image contains a polynomial ring of transcendence degree \(M_0\), while the incidence domain has dimension \(M_0\) by (10).  Since that domain is integral, the kernel is zero.  Each section therefore extends to a \(K_G\)-embedding
\[
 L\longrightarrow\operatorname{Frac}\mathbb C[[\xi]],
\]
where all embeddings use the same embedding of \(K_G\).  Their images of \(z_1\) have distinct constant terms, by the choice following (9).  The minimal polynomial of \(z_1\) over \(K_G\) consequently has at least \(2^d\) distinct roots in this common overfield.  Hence
\[
 [K_G(z_1):K_G]\geq2^d.
\tag{15}
\]
Together, (14) and (15) imply
\[
 [K_G(z_1):K_G]=[L:K_G]=2^d.
\tag{16}
\]
Thus \(d_{e^{\star}}(G^{\star}_{k,N})=2^{k+1}\), and this original coefficient separates all generic coordinate branches.  Because the ground field has characteristic zero, its minimal polynomial is separable.  Clearing its coefficient denominators and excluding their zeros together with its nonzero discriminant leaves a nonempty Zariski-open covariance set on which its \(2^d\) roots remain distinct.  The exact coordinate-image assertion in \(\mathrm{thm:incidence\mbox{-}localization}\) identifies those roots with precisely the finite queried-coordinate projection.

It remains to pass from \(N\) to any \(n>N\).  Append one fully bidirected child \(w\) of \(0\), as prescribed by \(\mathrm{def:attaining\mbox{-}family}\), and write \(x_w=\lambda_{0w}\) and \(s_w=(\sigma_{iw}:i\text{ is an old vertex},\sigma_{ww})\).  No new missing-bidirected residual involves \(w\).  Conditional on the old source coordinates and \(x_w\), covariance congruence is an invertible triangular polynomial change between the newly allowed disturbance coordinates and \(s_w\).  Therefore, if \(L_0,K_0\) are the old fields and \(L_1,K_1\) the new fields, then
\[
 L_1=L_0(x_w,s_w),
 \qquad
 K_1=K_0(s_w),
\tag{17}
\]
and the entries of \(s_w\) are algebraically independent over \(L_0(x_w)\), hence over \(L_0\).  If \(u_1,\ldots,u_{2^d}\) is a \(K_0\)-basis of \(K_0(z_1)\), any relation
\[
 \sum_j r_j(s_w)u_j=0,
 \qquad r_j(s_w)\in K_0(s_w),
\]
can be cleared of denominators.  Comparing coefficients of the algebraically independent monomials in \(s_w\) then gives only \(K_0\)-linear relations among the \(u_j\), so every \(r_j\) is zero.  The same basis also spans \(K_1(z_1)=K_0(z_1)(s_w)\) over \(K_1\).  Consequently
\[
 [K_1(z_1):K_1]=[K_0(z_1):K_0]=2^d.
\tag{18}
\]
Iterating (17)--(18) proves
\[
 d_{e^{\star}}(G^{\star}_{k,n})=2^{k+1}
 \qquad(n\geq2k+4).
\tag{19}
\]
The newly added arrow \(0\to w\) is placed in \(T\), so each iteration preserves the excess count \(k\), the arborescence property, and acyclicity.

Finally, \(d=k+1\geq1\) and \(n-2\geq2d\), whence
\[
 \binom{n-2}{2}\geq\binom{2d}{2}=d(2d-1)\geq d.
\]
The bound in \(\mathrm{thm:orientation\mbox{-}upper\mbox{-}bound}\) therefore gives \(D_k(n)\leq2^{k+1}\), while (19) and membership in \(\mathcal G_{n,k}\) give \(D_k(n)\geq2^{k+1}\).  Hence
\[
 D_k(n)=2^{k+1}\qquad(n\geq2k+4),
\]
and the nonempty Zariski-open separation assertion follows from the open set constructed above and its preservation under the purely transcendental padding in (17).
body.justification: A uniform attaining region turns the exponent from a loose Bezout count into a sharp coordinate frontier for a substantial size range.
body.gap: Foygel, Draisma, and Drton already exhibit cubic and quartic behavior in small SEMs, but not an all-\(k\) family with one edge separating \(2^{k+1}\) generic branches.
body.consumer: Software maintainers obtain adversarial benchmark families and users obtain a worst-case ambiguity warning indexed by the number of added parents.
